title: Runtime Interlock & Kernel Safety: Operator Manual
author: Mariana Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose: This manual documents the runtime interlock and kernel safety mechanisms used by Redwood's serving runtime and provides operator procedures for diagnosing, mitigating, and recovering from incidents that involve kernel scheduling, cross-kernel handoffs, and fidelity-preserving fallback. It combines high-level architecture context with prescriptive runbooks, profiling/benchmarking steps, and rollout guidance.

Audience: Oncall SREs, runtime engineers, release engineers, and third-party accelerator integrators.

Summary: The runtime interlock is a thin coordination layer that mediates kernel lifecycle operations (start/stop/slice/handoff) and enforces safety invariants (memory isolation, KV cache consistency, credit accounting). Kernel scheduling safety modes (Strict, Graceful, Soft) define how preemption, eviction, and fallback behave under pressure. This doc explains operator-visible signals, safe mitigation pathways, and how to run targeted perf/quality experiments before/after changes.

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner_team: engineering (serving-runtime squad)
- Pager duty: serving-runtime-oncall
- Escalation list: runtime-tech-lead@redwood.ai, infra-sre-lead@redwood.ai, product-reliability@redwood.ai

SLOs and Safety Thresholds

Table: Key SLOs and operational thresholds
| Signal | SLO / Threshold | Action if exceeded | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| P50 request latency (short seq) | < 50ms | Monitor; no action | runtime-observability |
| P99 tail latency | < 600ms | Investigate kernel queueing; run preemption audit | oncall |
| Kernel backlog depth | < 120 queued slots | Activate graceful mode; migrate cohorts | runtime-op |
| Total GPU mem usage per node | < 92% | Evict opportunistic cohorts | capacity-planning |
| KV cache miss rate | < 8% | Trigger KV warmup policy | model-serving |
| Kernel soft-failure rate | < 0.1% | Auto-retry; if >1% escalate | oncall |

Design and Architecture Notes

- Interlock role: The interlock sits between the dispatcher and kernel manager. It validates admission, attaches safety tokens (credit, cohort id), and annotates each slot with fidelity and rollback metadata. It also emits the canonical decision trace for later repro.
- Kernel safety assertions: each kernel exposes a safety contract: {memory_budget, allowed_quant_modes, preemptibility, kv_consistency_hint}. The interlock verifies contracts before scheduling.
- Scheduling surfaces: admission controller, slot allocator, kernel handoff API, eviction coordinator. Each has a small set of operator-visible flags exposed via /api/internal/admin and metrics with _safety suffix.

Kernel Scheduling Safety Modes

1) Strict Mode (default for Dedicated):
- No preemption for in-flight requests; admission rejects if not enough contiguous memory.
- Use when tenant requires deterministic latency and no fidelity changes.
- Operator actions: preserve, do not evict, raise capacity request if backlog sustained.

2) Graceful Mode (default for Hosted burst):
- Allows cooperative preemption: kernels complete current micro-batch then yield.
- Eviction results in fallback to a pinned model variant (quantized or smaller).
- Operator actions: monitor fallback rate, check quality regression dashboards.

3) Soft Mode (default for low-cost tiers):
- Aggressive eviction + immediate hedged routing to cheaper variants.
- Best-effort KV cache preservation; higher miss rate tolerated.
- Operator actions: tune economic governor thresholds and watch token-level cost signals.

Operator Runbooks (high-level decision tree)

Incident triage summary: For latency spikes or kernel failures follow the numbered steps below. Treat production degradation as in_priority until resolved.

1) Identify scope:
  a) Run: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ADMIN_TOKEN}" https://admin.internal/runtime/signals?window=5m | jq .summary
  b) Check metrics: kernel_backlog, kernel_miss_rate, gpu_mem_util, kv_miss_rate, fallback_rate.

2) Rapid mitigation (first 3 minutes):
  a) If gpu_mem_util > 95% on nodes and kernel_backlog > 150: set scheduler to Graceful for affected cluster:
     - CLI: rwctl scheduler set-mode --cluster prod-eu-1 --mode graceful --reason "emergency memory pressure"
  b) If kernel soft-failure rate spikes: increase kernel retry multiplier to 3x and open incident.
  c) If P99 latency > target and fallback_rate rising: temporarily raise admission threshold for opportunistic cohorts to 0 to reduce noise.

3) Containment (3–30 minutes):
  - Trigger KV-cache aggressive warmup on hot cohorts: rwctl kvcache warmup --cohort <cohort-id> --target-size 80%
  - Rebalance heavy cohorts to nodes with spare GPU availability: rwctl cluster rebalance --source <node> --dest <node-list>
  - If a kernel binary is suspected: roll a canary rollback to previous kernel version in a small cohort. See Rollback steps below.

4) Recovery and postmortem preparation (30–120 minutes):
  - Restore scheduler to previous mode once backlog reduced and mem utilization below 88%.
  - Save decision traces: /var/log/runtime/decision-traces/<inc-id>.ndjson and attach to ticket.
  - Annotate incident with kernel metrics, trace ids, and any manual interventions.

Escalation Criteria

- If fallback_rate > 3% sustained for 15 minutes -> page runtime-tech-lead.
- If node GPU mem remains > 95% for 20 minutes after mitigations -> page infra-sre-lead.
- If kernel panic or node reboot occurs -> follow hardware incident playbook (eng-infra).

Profiling and Benchmarking Procedures

Purpose: Provide repeatable steps to profile a kernel interaction and validate safety changes.

1) Controlled profiling with shadow traffic
  - Prepare a mirrored workload with 1% traffic (shadow channel) and tag with experiment id. Use the shadow harness described in the benchmarking-suite (see related pages).
  - Commands:
     - Start mirror: rwctl mirror start --source-route /v1/generate --rate 1% --label safety-test-<id>
     - Enable kernel tracing: rwctl trace enable --kernel <kernel-id> --sample-rate 100% --out /tmp/trace-<id>.json

2) Kernel microbench
  - Run the microbenchmark runner on an isolated node with identical kernel parameters:
    - ./bench/kernel_runner --kernel-revision <rev> --seq-len 64 --batch-shapes "[1,2,4,8]" --samples 2000 --out perf-<id>.csv
  - Capture CPU/GPU counters using perf/NVTX: nvprof or nvidia-smi dmon and the telemetry bridge.

3) Observability checklist
  - Ensure traces include: admission_decision, kernel_hint, kv_prefetch_hint, preemption_window, fidelity_tag.
  - Confirm parity between shadow and production decision traces for a sample of requests.

4) Quality gate
  - Run prompt-set evaluation: take 500 sampled prompts spanning short/long/interactive flows and compare outputs across candidate kernels. Gate criteria: median ROUGE-L difference < 0.6 and hallucination signal delta < 0.8 (per eval harness).

Release/Cutover Checklist for Kernel or Interlock Changes

1) Preflight
  - Verify unit tests and scheduler simulator pass in CI.
  - Create a benchmark artifact with microbenchmark CSVs and a decision-trace sample. Attach to PR.
  - Author a short rollout plan with canary cohort ids and rollback criteria.

2) Canary (internal)
  - Canary cohort size: 1–2% traffic in mirrored mode for 30 minutes. Monitor kernel soft-failure, fallback_rate, kv_miss_rate, P99 latency.
  - Required signoff: runtime lead, bench team, and model-onboarding reviewer.

3) Gradual ramp
  - Ramp using traffic slices: 5% -> 15% -> 40% -> 100% with 30–60 minute steady windows.
  - At each ramp step validate: no >10% increase in fallback_rate, no >2x increase in kernel soft-failures, P99 within SLO.

4) Rollback
  - Immediate rollback command: rwctl kernel rollback --target <kernel-id> --to-rev <rev> --force-restart 0
  - If rollback does not reduce failures, switch scheduler to Strict and divert traffic to a known-good region.

Known Issues (operator-facing)

- Large-model eviction oscillation (INC-2026-034): Under mixed short/long workloads some cohorts constantly oscillate between eviction and warmstart, increasing tail latency. Mitigation: enable epoch-based eviction window and increase KV warmup weight for affected cohorts.
- Heterogeneous quant-mode mismatch (KERNEL-QUANT-12): Some kernels compile with a quant-mode that causes higher tensor-conversion overhead under small batch shapes. Workaround: pin quant-mode=dynamic for small-batch kernels till patch.
- Tracer overhead under 100% sampling (TRACE-OVERHEAD-07): Enabling 100% kernel tracing on busy nodes can itself increase latency. Use 10% stratified sampling for live traffic; reserve 100% for isolated profiling nodes.

Appendix: Operator Commands and Policy Snippets

Example scheduler policy (YAML)
|---
cluster: prod-eu-1
policy:
  admission:
    max_backlog: 120
    reserve_quota: 6
  eviction:
    mode: graceful
    epoch_window: 28s
  fidelity_governor:
    soft_threshold: 0.03
    hard_threshold: 0.08
|---

CLI quick reference
- rwctl scheduler set-mode --cluster <cluster> --mode <strict|graceful|soft> --reason "<text>"
- rwctl kvcache warmup --cohort <id> --target-size <percent>
- rwctl trace enable --kernel <id> --sample-rate <0-100> --out <file>
- rwctl kernel rollback --target <kernel-id> --to-rev <rev> --force-restart <0|1>

Decision-trace example (NDJSON line)
{"ts":"2026-02-18T12:34:56Z","req_id":"r-abc123","decision":{"admit":true,"kernel":"k-42","fidelity_tag":"q8-dyn","kv_hint":true}}

Operator tips and heuristics

- Before changing admission thresholds, always run the admission simulator with a shadow workload for at least 15 minutes.
- When investigating KV miss spikes, correlate with model-onboarding events; new model versions often have cold KV footprints.
- Use node annotations to mark hardware pressure and avoid automatic rebalancing for nodes undergoing infra maintenance.

Post-incident artifacts to collect

1) Kernel trace files (/tmp/trace-*.json)
2) Decision traces for the incident window (/var/log/runtime/decision-traces/<inc-id>.ndjson)
3) Perf CSVs and NVTX exports from the microbench run
4) Rollout and change history (PR ids, CI artifacts)
